title: A plasma-magnet sail that takes useful delta-v from the solar wind

concept.text: A plasma-magnet sail would propel a spacecraft by taking momentum from the solar wind, the flowing plasma emitted by the Sun. Driven currents in plasma around the spacecraft would sustain an extended magnetic structure that deflects the incoming flow. For propulsion to work, the resulting force must transfer back to the spacecraft. The effective obstacle could be much larger than the spacecraft without requiring a solid sail of the same size.

The plasma magnet is a variant of a magnetic sail: it uses driven plasma currents in place of a massive current-carrying sail coil. Its proposed advantage is a large interaction area with comparatively modest onboard equipment and electrical power. The innovation sought here is sustained, useful spacecraft acceleration from that interaction in the real solar wind. Laboratory momentum transfer and calculations of large magnetic structures are steps toward this capability, rather than demonstrations of a working cruise propulsion system.

significance.text: If sustained operation were demonstrated with favorable spacecraft-level performance, a plasma magnet could obtain propulsive momentum and energy from the surrounding solar-wind flow while using little onboard propellant. That could reduce the amount of reaction mass a spacecraft must carry for a given mission. Slough’s NIAC report projects magnetic structures tens of kilometres across and multi-megawatt thrust power with modest onboard electrical power. Such power would be drawn from interaction with the external flow; the projections do not establish an achieved propulsion efficiency or flight performance.

Rapid travel to the outer solar system is a potential application, conditional on adequate acceleration, endurance, power supply, spacecraft mass, and usable trajectories. A first demonstration of useful delta-v would establish an initial propulsion capability, but would not by itself establish shorter mission times than chemical or solar-electric propulsion. The report also discusses crewed potential; neither crewed suitability nor a categorical need for a separate propulsion system on every crewed mission follows from the available evidence.

The surrounding flow also imposes a limit. For passive acceleration by a pushing solar wind, the available interaction weakens as the spacecraft approaches the wind’s speed. The NIAC report describes solar-wind speeds of roughly 350–800 km/s as the proposed ultimate speed scale, rather than a demonstrated cruise speed. Exceeding the pushing wind’s speed would require an additional propulsion mechanism or energy source. Braking against a planetary plasma environment or the interstellar medium is a separate prospective application that needs its own coupling and mission analysis.

Conceptual comparison: a photon sail exchanges momentum with light, whereas this concept exchanges momentum with flowing plasma. Both can draw on an external resource, but their force mechanisms and operating limits differ. The analogy does not establish plasma-magnet readiness, and the supplied inspectable evidence does not independently establish the research’s claim about flown photon sails.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target breakthrough is a space measurement showing that a deployed plasma magnet produces useful thrust from the real solar wind. The laboratory results do not establish that a kilometre-scale or larger magnetic structure can inflate, maintain a suitable equilibrium, deflect enough incoming plasma, and transmit the resulting momentum to a spacecraft continuously for days. These are coupled requirements: producing a magnetic structure alone would not demonstrate useful propulsion.

A central scientific barrier is establishing that laboratory scaling applies to the space environment. The NIAC report describes its current-carrying laboratory plasma as relatively collisionless, even near the antennas. Its separate finding that the experiment remained in a kinetic regime with incomplete ion deflection should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that the bench test was simply collisional. The unresolved issue is whether the relevant plasma and magnetic length scales, current formation, and momentum coupling support the projected space-scale behavior.

Engineering synthesis: a practical system would also need to sustain and control the plasma currents, quantify any plasma or propellant replenishment, and maintain useful thrust as solar-wind conditions change. Its electrical power demand, total hardware mass, force direction, and operating lifetime must be measured together. A large magnetic interaction region would be insufficient if the resources needed to maintain it erased the spacecraft-level benefit.

current_state.text: John Slough’s NIAC Phase II final report, The Plasma Magnet, describes laboratory tests using a solar-wind simulator with a characteristic flow speed of about 50 km/s. Its summary reports a ballistic-pendulum measurement of approximately 1.25 N average thrust during a 200-microsecond pulse. This is evidence of reported laboratory momentum transfer during a short pulse, not sustained thrust on a spacecraft in the solar wind.

The summary also reports about 0.6 MW of thrust power. That figure needs reconciliation: multiplying the stated 1.25 N force by the stated 50 km/s flow speed gives 62.5 kW, or 0.0625 MW, approximately a factor of ten lower. This arithmetic identifies an inconsistency in the supplied account; it does not determine whether the report used another velocity, another definition of power, or an erroneous number. The reported force and pulse duration should be retained without treating the 0.6 MW figure as a resolved conversion.

The report says the laboratory system remained in the kinetic regime and that ion deflection was incomplete. It recommends a large-tank experiment or a microsatellite demonstration to confirm scaling for deep-space operation. The roughly 30 km magnetic structure and multi-megawatt space performance described in the earlier research are scaling projections, not measured space results. The report itself acknowledges that substantial experimental and theoretical work is needed to substantiate the scaling.

The supplied review had access to a report extraction that ends during page 70; the detailed later thrust material and figures were not inspected. The earlier research assigns the report a performance period of 1 October 2004 through 30 September 2006, but the review could not establish that interval from the available extract. Those dates remain an attribution from the research rather than independently confirmed report metadata.

The earlier research identifies Development of a 3U Plasma Magnet Technology Demonstrator, attributed to Oliver B. Guy, Andrew J. Higgins, Jeff Greason, and coauthors, as AIAA 2026-2216, published online on 8 January 2026. It reports that the abstract proposes a 3U demonstrator and says the plasma magnet had yet to be demonstrated in space. The research records abstract-only access behind an AIAA access wall. No saved text or document artifact was available to the supplied review, so the paper’s metadata and abstract claims could not be independently verified there. It remains a reported design proposal, not evidence of a completed flight.

For the related electric sail, the earlier research identifies a paper by Lachlan Goulden and colleagues in Physics of Plasmas 32, 063511, reportedly published on 20 June 2025. It describes a force measurement on a negatively charged electric sail using pulsed copper cathodic-arc plasma in a laboratory. If accurately described, that experiment concerns electrostatic coupling in a laboratory plasma, not a solar-wind cruise or plasma-magnet flight. The research also attributes a first-published-force-measurement claim to the authors. No saved artifact was available to the supplied review, leaving the experimental details, publication metadata, and priority claim unverified there.

The earlier research additionally describes a 2026 electric-sail conference abstract, seen as a PDF extract, concerning a ground campaign and making a broad statement about the absence of earlier force demonstrations. No URL or artifact for that abstract was supplied, so its scope and relationship to the reported 2025 result remain unresolved. More generally, the supplied material contains no usable recent search record establishing whether a plasma-magnet flight had been reported by 1 November 2026. This gap prevents a categorical statement about current flight absence; it does not invalidate the historical laboratory findings.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed milestone: a spacecraft deploys a plasma magnet and accumulates at least 1 km/s of delta-v attributable to interaction with the solar wind. This threshold is a proposed useful first cruise demonstration, not an established standard. Whether it is feasible and convincingly detectable depends on spacecraft mass, operating duration, tracking precision, and the force model.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed milestone

completion_criteria.text: Proposed attribution test: publish tracking data and an uncertainty analysis that distinguish the measured acceleration from onboard propellant expenditure, solar-photon pressure, and other relevant forces. Record local solar-wind conditions alongside magnetic-field extent, electrical power, operating modes, and all plasma or propellant consumption. Where feasible, repeated activation and deactivation would help establish whether the force changes with plasma-magnet operation and with the measured external flow.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed attribution test

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and endurance test: repeat the thrust measurement across multiple operating periods and solar-wind conditions, allow independent analysis of the data, and seek replication on another instrumented spacecraft. Demonstrate sustained operation on the days-long timescale needed to address the gap between short laboratory pulses and cruise propulsion. Report the demonstrated range of conditions and failures; finite tests would establish operating breadth within that range, not universal performance in every plasma environment.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and endurance test

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: assess useful delta-v together with total system mass, power demand, consumables, controllability, and lifetime. A successful first flight would establish the capability measured under its tested conditions. Claims of rapid outer-system travel, sustained megawatt performance, braking in other plasma environments, or crewed applicability would require additional demonstrations and mission analysis.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed practical boundary

related_concepts.text: Magnetic sails and electric sails are the closest architectural relatives. A conventional magnetic sail uses a current-carrying coil, while a plasma magnet sustains its extended magnetic structure through driven plasma currents. An electric sail instead uses charged wires and electrostatic forces to interact with flowing plasma. These approaches overlap in seeking momentum from an external plasma flow, but a successful plasma-magnet flight would not validate electric-sail hardware or its force model. The electric sail remains a related architecture within this record, without changing ROC-06’s identity.

Roster comparison, based on the supplied concept descriptions: ROC-03, a directed-energy lightsail accelerated to a substantial fraction of light speed, also obtains momentum externally, but from a directed light beam rather than ambient solar-wind plasma. ROC-02, beamed-energy launch of a useful payload into orbit, likewise depends on externally supplied energy while addressing launch. Neither capability follows from demonstrating a plasma magnet, whose pushing-flow speed limit differs from the operating constraints of a beam-driven system.

Roster comparison, based on the supplied concept descriptions: ROC-01, sustained air-breathing combined-cycle flight to orbital speed, concerns atmospheric ascent and engine transitions. ROC-04, an open-cycle gas-core nuclear rocket, and ROC-05, a fission-fragment rocket, concern onboard nuclear propulsion with distinct mechanisms for producing thrust. ROC-06 instead targets momentum exchange with ambient plasma in space. Success in any one would leave the others’ central engineering demonstrations outstanding.

Roster comparison, based on the supplied concept descriptions: ROC-07, an operational momentum-exchange tether, transfers momentum through a physical tether to move payloads between orbits. It overlaps with ROC-06 in obtaining payload momentum through interaction with an external system, but its deployment, structural, and orbital requirements are different. ROC-08, industrial-scale production and loading of rocket propellant off Earth, supplies consumables for propulsion systems. A successful plasma magnet might reduce propellant needs for particular cruise phases, while leaving off-Earth propellant production useful for other maneuvers and vehicles. These remain separate innovations.

change_log.change: Preserved ROC-06 and its title while explaining plasma currents, magnetic deflection, and momentum transfer to the spacecraft.
change_log.reason: The research and review support a coherent propulsion concept despite unresolved performance and flight-status claims.

change_log.change: Replaced the blanket description of the laboratory test as collisional with the report’s distinction between relatively collisionless current-carrying plasma and kinetic-regime incomplete ion deflection.
change_log.reason: Collisionality and kinetic scaling are different scientific issues, and the earlier characterization conflicts with the reviewed passage.

change_log.change: Retained the reported 1.25 N force, 200-microsecond pulse, 50 km/s simulator speed, and 0.6 MW power statement while exposing the numerical discrepancy.
change_log.reason: The reviewed summary supports these reported values, but force multiplied by the stated speed gives 0.0625 MW; the correct reconciliation is unknown.

change_log.change: Separated laboratory findings from projections of roughly 30 km structures and multi-megawatt space performance.
change_log.reason: Scaling calculations do not establish sustained spacecraft propulsion.

change_log.change: Preserved later-paper descriptions and dates as attributed research accounts, with their access and verification limitations.
change_log.reason: Useful context should remain available without implying that the supplied review verified missing documents or abstracts.

change_log.change: Removed the categorical assertion that no plasma-magnet flight had been reported by the reference date.
change_log.reason: The supplied recent evidence and search record do not establish absence as of 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Qualified propellantlessness, outer-system travel times, braking possibilities, and crewed implications.
change_log.reason: These consequences depend on consumables, spacecraft-level performance, environment-specific coupling, and mission analysis.

change_log.change: Retained the proposed 1 km/s milestone and added uncertainty analysis, local wind measurements, reproducibility, endurance, and practical operating boundaries.
change_log.reason: Useful delta-v must be attributable to solar-wind interaction, and the threshold is a proposal whose detectability and feasibility remain design-dependent.

change_log.change: Explained electric-sail overlap and distinctions across the full supplied roster without merging entries.
change_log.reason: Shared external momentum or energy does not make different propulsion mechanisms interchangeable or allow one demonstration to validate another.

unresolved_issues: What definition, velocity, or correction reconciles the NIAC report’s 0.6 MW thrust-power statement with 1.25 N and 50 km/s?
The available report extraction ends during page 70, and detailed later thrust material and figures were not inspected. Their contribution to interpreting the measurements remains unknown.
The stated 1 October 2004–30 September 2006 report performance period was not established by the supplied review.

The AIAA demonstrator paper and AIP electric-sail paper lack saved artifacts in the supplied evidence. Their reported dates, abstract contents, experimental details, and priority statements remain unverified by that review.
The described 2026 electric-sail conference abstract has no supplied URL or artifact. Its scope and relationship to the reported 2025 measurement remain unresolved.
Whether a plasma-magnet space demonstration had been reported by 1 November 2026 cannot be determined from the supplied material.
Space-scale inflation, equilibrium, force transfer, control, endurance, and consumable requirements remain to be demonstrated together.
The feasibility and measurement confidence of a 1 km/s first-flight milestone require a specific spacecraft and mission design.
Rapid outer-system missions, braking in other plasma environments, and crewed applications require evidence beyond an initial useful delta-v demonstration.
